settings.editor: Semen analysis and sperm preparation for IUI, done at Dr. Jawaria Rasheed’s clinic so couples can complete fertility tests and treatment in one place.

Male factors play a part in many couples’ difficulty conceiving, so a fertility check always looks at both partners. The clinic’s andrology lab tests the semen sample and prepares sperm for IUI, and Dr. Jawaria explains every report to you in person.

icon_list.text: Semen analysis (count, movement and shape of sperm)
Repeat and follow-up semen tests
Sperm washing and preparation for IUI
Same-day IUI with the prepared sample
Reports explained clearly by the doctor

settings.editor:
A semen analysis is a simple, painless test. The lab looks at:

  • Volume — how much semen there is
  • Sperm concentration — how many sperm there are per millilitre
  • Motility — how well the sperm move
  • Morphology — the shape of the sperm
  • Other checks when needed, such as vitality or signs of infection

Results are compared with the reference values in the World Health Organization (WHO) laboratory manual for semen examination. Sperm quality naturally changes from one sample to the next, so one abnormal result does not mean infertility — the test is usually repeated after a few weeks before any decision is made.

settings.title: How to prepare for the test

settings.editor:
• Avoid ejaculation for 2 to 7 days before the test.
  • The sample is collected by masturbation into a clean container given by the lab, in a private room at the clinic.
  • Do not use lubricants, saliva or a condom — they can harm the sperm.
  • Collect the whole sample; if any part is lost, tell the lab staff.
  • Tell the doctor about any fever or illness in the last 3 months and any medicines you take, as these can affect the result.
  • If you were asked to collect the sample at home, bring it to the lab within about an hour, kept close to body temperature. Please ask the clinic first.

On the day of IUI, the husband gives a fresh sample at the clinic. In the lab, the sample is washed and concentrated: the seminal fluid is removed and the healthiest, most active sperm are separated into a small volume. Dr. Jawaria then places this prepared sample directly into the uterus with a thin, soft catheter. Preparation takes a short while, so couples usually wait at the clinic.

settings.title: Your IUI day, step by step

settings.editor:
1. Fertility check

Both partners are assessed, including a semen analysis.

2. Follicle monitoring

Ultrasound scans track the growing egg follicle.

3. Timing

IUI is planned for the time of ovulation.

4. Sample & preparation

A fresh sample is given and prepared in the lab.

5. IUI

The prepared sperm are placed in the uterus. It takes a few minutes.

6. Pregnancy test

A test is done about two weeks later, as advised.
Every sample is labelled and checked against the couple’s identity at each step. Collection is private, and results are shared only with you and your doctor.

seo_description: Regular check-ups, scans and guidance from early pregnancy until delivery. Consultant gynecologist Dr. Jawaria Rasheed in Bahawalpur.

settings.editor: Antenatal care means regular check-ups during pregnancy to look after the health of both mother and baby. Good antenatal care finds problems early, keeps you informed at every stage and prepares you for a safe delivery.

Every pregnancy is different. Some mothers have a smooth journey, while others need closer monitoring because of high blood pressure, diabetes, anaemia, thyroid problems or difficulties in a previous pregnancy. Regular visits with an experienced gynecologist mean these issues are picked up early and managed safely.

Dr. Jawaria Rasheed provides antenatal care in Bahawalpur from the first positive test through to planning your delivery, with clear advice on diet, supplements, activity and the warning signs every mother should know.

settings.title: When to book your first pregnancy visit

icon_list.text: You have a positive pregnancy test (ideally before 8–10 weeks)
You are planning a pregnancy and want advice beforehand
You had a miscarriage, premature birth or caesarean section before
You have diabetes, high blood pressure, thyroid disease or epilepsy
You are expecting twins, or are under 18 or over 35
You conceived after fertility treatment such as IUI

settings.editor:
• Confirming the pregnancy and calculating your due date.
  • Blood tests for blood group, haemoglobin, blood sugar, thyroid and infections, as advised.
  • Ultrasound scans at the right stages to check the baby’s growth and position.
  • Routine checks of blood pressure, weight and urine at each visit.
  • Advice on nutrition, supplements, rest, exercise and travel.

First trimester (up to 12 weeks)

Dating scan, booking tests, folic acid, and help with nausea and tiredness.

Second trimester (13–27 weeks)

Anomaly scan, iron and calcium review, blood sugar testing when advised.

Third trimester (28 weeks onwards)

Growth checks, baby’s movements, blood pressure monitoring and delivery planning.

High-risk pregnancy

Closer follow-up for diabetes, high blood pressure, twins or previous complications.

Most mothers are seen about once a month until 28 weeks, every two weeks until 36 weeks and then weekly until delivery. Your schedule may be adjusted to your health and your baby’s needs.

Bring your antenatal file, reports and scans to every visit, and note any questions in advance.

• Eat a balanced diet with protein, fruit, vegetables, dairy and whole grains.
  • Drink plenty of water and rest when you feel tired.
  • Take only the medicines prescribed for you — check before taking anything new, including herbal remedies.
  • Stay active with gentle walking unless advised otherwise.
  • Avoid smoking and second-hand smoke.
  • Keep your antenatal file with you when you travel.

settings.title: Common conditions that need extra care

settings.editor: Anaemia is very common in pregnancy and is treated with iron. Gestational diabetes is high blood sugar that develops during pregnancy; it is found by a blood sugar test and controlled with diet and sometimes medicine. High blood pressure and pre-eclampsia need close monitoring because they can affect both mother and baby. Regular check-ups are the best way to pick these up early.

Cervical cancer is one of the few cancers that can largely be prevented. Most cases are linked to long-term infection with high-risk types of human papillomavirus (HPV). The changes it causes develop slowly over years — which gives screening time to catch them.

Many women in Pakistan have never had a Pap smear. The test takes a few minutes and is done in privacy by Dr. Jawaria Rasheed, a female consultant gynecologist in Bahawalpur.

Who should have screening?

  • Married or sexually active women, from the age advised by your doctor
  • Women who have never been screened
  • Women due for a repeat test
  • Follow-up after a previous abnormal result

Symptoms that need examination (not just screening)

  • Bleeding between periods or after intercourse
  • Bleeding after menopause
  • Persistent, unusual or blood-stained discharge
  • Pelvic pain

These symptoms should be checked even if a recent Pap smear was normal.

What happens during the test

  • Privacy: the test is done in a private room with a female doctor.
  • Speculum: a smooth instrument gently opens the vagina to see the cervix.
  • Sample: a small brush collects cells — this takes a few seconds.
  • Lab test: the sample is checked for abnormal cells and, where available, HPV.

Understanding your result

Normal

Continue routine screening at the interval your doctor advises.

Minor changes

Often a repeat test or HPV test after some months, as many changes settle on their own.

Higher-grade changes

Colposcopy (a closer look at the cervix) and treatment of abnormal areas, usually by referral.

Preparing for your Pap smear

  • Book when you are not on your period.
  • Avoid intercourse, vaginal creams or douching for two days before the test.
  • You can return to normal activities straight away. Light spotting is possible.

HPV vaccination, where available, helps protect girls and young women from future cervical cancer.

About HPV

Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a very common virus. Most infections clear on their own within one to two years without causing problems. In a small number of women, high-risk types persist and can slowly cause changes in the cervix. Screening finds these changes, and HPV vaccination given to girls before exposure greatly reduces the risk.

What is colposcopy?

If a Pap smear shows significant changes, a colposcopy may be advised. It is a closer examination of the cervix using a magnifying instrument. It feels similar to a Pap smear. Small samples (biopsies) may be taken, and abnormal areas can often be treated with a simple procedure.

Reducing your risk

  • Attend screening when due, even if you feel well.
  • Get your daughters vaccinated against HPV where available.
  • Do not smoke — smoking increases the risk of cervical changes.
  • See a doctor about any unusual bleeding.
